{{Feature|informative|It is possible to change the artwork in all the frames and on all the canvases that arrived with the [[Arma_3_Art_of_War|Arma 3 Art of War DLC]]. This can be achieved directly in the Eden Editor by accessing the asset's attributes and adjusting the relative path to the texture. It can also be done via the [[setObjectTexture]] script command or [[BIS_fnc_setObjectTexture]] function. For more information on replacing textures in-game, see the article on [[Retexturing with setObjectTexture]]. For texture reference layouts, see the second table at the bottom of this page.}}

| 3rd Place - 2D Art Category
| Entry Hall, North Wall
| In this playful yet provocative scene, a paramedic carries a wounded individual on a stretcher while a pair of Livonian soldiers look on. The laptop reads 'EMP', an acronym for ElectroMagnetic Pulse. EMP weapons destroy electronics and are sometimes used indiscriminately in cyberwarfare, breaking International Humanitarian Law by targeting civilian as well as military infrastructure.

2020

| Entry Hall, North Wall
| Although it might appear like science fiction, this busy combat scene presages an authentic glimpse of tomorrow’s battlefields. Urban environments, swarming with ground and aerial combat drones, autonomous medical units, and soldiers, clad in dehumanizing armor, strike us now as a grounded interpretation of what is to come. The legal and humanitarian challenges these new forms of warfare present are a pressing global concern.

2028

| Screenshot Category Winner
| Entry Hall, East Wall
| Not all wars are fought upon the battlefield. This photograph depicts the famous 1989 'Blue Party Prison Riot' at Andrzejów Detention Center in Livonia, an episode which made international headlines and quickly captured the imagination of the world. Inmates, along with several guards, in solidarity with national actions against the Soviet regime and angry with deteriorating living conditions, staged several weeks of protests before finally taking full control of the facility.

1989

Photograph (Andrzejów, Livonia)

| Entry Hall, East Wall
| Combat aircraft led to a revolution in the way that wars were waged, defining many conflicts over the last 100 years. But what will be the next seismic shift in warfare? What will be the 21st Century’s ‘Guernica’? A sky, dark with unmanned bombers? Clouds of miniature drones, subjugating nations at the touch of a button? Or will aerial engagements become a thing of the past, slowly superseded by battles in space?

2003

Photograph (Kaiserslautern, Germany)

| De Kornelis Zaal, South Wall
| This touching photograph is a powerful reminder of how armed conflict can impact children. Aside from the nightmarish imagery, embodied here by faceless soldiers in hazmat suits, war causes intense psychological trauma through the severance of emotional and physical ties. The experiences of young victims, forced to abandon homes and loved ones, often transcend generations and inflict indiscernible wounds, many of which remain for life.

2035

Photograph (La Roche, Horizon Islands)

| De Kornelis Zaal, West Wall
| Like the rows of military graves in cemeteries across the world, this sober image highlights the human cost of conflict in no uncertain terms. In the context of modern warfare, it also poses some difficult questions. Not only in relation to reasons for war but with regards to the methods of waging it. Are autonomous weapons, for instance, an opportunity to save soldiers' lives? Do we really want to remove these tragic consequences, allowing nations to project force with impunity? And how can we argue against robots on the battlefield with the loved ones of combatants who have made an ultimate, yet ultimately avoidable sacrifice? Perhaps, scenes like this one, are a necessary reality of war?

2035

|| De Kornelis Zaal, West Wall
| In this famous work of abstract art, we are offered a chillingly prophetic vision of future conflict. Simply entitled 'Gray Goo', it alludes to the gray, slime-like appearance of molecular nanotechnology. Once a hypothetical concept, it became the controversial subject of military study in 2033. Today, propelled by recent breakthroughs in quantum technology, the idea of a globous and self-replicating mass of tiny robots, capable of stripping away the strongest steel, is edging from science fiction to science fact. Faced with such realities, many argue that International Humanitarian Law has a moral and legal responsibility to regulate new technologies.

| Portrait of the Dutch philanthropist and founder of the International Development &amp;amp; Aid Project, Lars Blanken. The wealthy son of a shipbuilding tycoon and war profiteer, Blanken turned his back on the pursuit of profit and became an instrumental figure in the Refugee Council, based in Leiden, supporting the Belgian diaspora through the First World War. This gallery is named in his honor. Visitors may notice the inscription on the fresco around the glass rotunda. It is a reference to Blanken's famous quote: 'Gentlemen, man's humanity has been weighed and found wanting - but <t font='RobotoCondensedBold'>together we can tip the scales.

| The cluster of menacing robotic soldiers in this work, standing against the bright orange glow of a featureless city aflame, are in fact, allowing enemy combatants to pull a wounded comrade to safety. Are these faceless entities observing the spirit of International Humanitarian Law? Do they suggest a coming era of restraint in modern warfare, free of human folly and passions? Or is this simply indifference? A short, calculating pause before an algorithm loads and the systematic killing continues? Like the future itself, this piece presents us with a vision that is difficult to decipher.

| This screenshot from a military simulation game raises some important questions regarding the fetishization of violence in popular culture. Are we becoming desensitized to representations of conflict? Or are video games and other interactive media a lens for exploring real-world concerns and unpleasant realities, challenging preconceptions and perspectives? This last point, remains divisive.

| De Verbeek Kamer, East Wall
| The sharp contrasts, post-processing effects, and angular shadows that dissect this scene perfectly echo the intensity of the chaotic situation, as experienced by the soldiers. Each combatant crouches behind cover and seemingly melds with their environment, as if swallowed by the hostile surroundings. The enemy is nowhere to be seen. However, the non-presence is a presence in itself and brilliantly communicates feelings of unease and tension. The photograph also addresses an increasing trend in modern conflict; the urbanization of the battlefield. Consequently, it seems both familiar and contemporary.

2012

Photograph (Zargabad, Takistan)

| Screenshot Category Winner
| De Verbeek Kamer, West Wall
| The human cost of war is cleverly executed in this clear but effective digital image. On close inspection, we can see that the ghostly silhouettes of the dead represent the losses of all sides and factions; spirits of fallen comrades appear to mingle with those of the enemy and all appear to be accompanying the grieving soldier in the mid-ground. The chiaroscuro effect is also ingeniously used, separating the living from the dead by way of light and shade.

| A much neglected aspect of war art concerns the conceptualization of ideas. Although many of us would accept the 15th Century scribblings of Leonardo da Vinci's siege weapons and fighting vehicles as art, contemporary works draw more complex reactions. Could it be our appreciation of innovative designs is tempered by their destructive potential? Or are there qualities in paintings such as this, that transcend their immediate application?
